newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stocks seen heading higher at open.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stocks seen heading higher at open.

text.p: Wall Street stocks are expected to head higher at the open Wednesday, barring any indications of higher inflation in the February consumer price index due to be released at 0830 EST/1330 GMT.
High techs may lose ground at the open regardless of the data after bearish articles in the Wall Street Journal and New York Times this morning.
"Based on what I can see right now, we will have a higher opening. Of course, a lot depends on the CPI," said Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments.
"Now that the unwinding of options has taken hold, the market will concentrate on economic news and the CPI will lead the way," Cardillo said.

The CPI, excluding food and energy, is forecast to rise by 0.2 percent in February following a 0.1 percent increase the previous month. The overall CPI figure is expected to do the same. Sharply higher-than-forecast data would increase fears that the U.S. Federal Reserve could decide to push up interest rates at its March 25 Federal Open Market Committee meeting.
Data have had a strong impact on day-to-day volatility in stocks, resulting in large single-session swings.
In Tokyo, the Nikkei Average was up 48.51 points, or 0.26 percent, at 18,493.71.
In London, the FTSE 100 Index was down 3.9 at 4352.9

Among U.S. shares traded in London Compaq Computer Corp slipped $1/2 to $74-3/8, Microsoft Corp , eased $1/2 to $99-1/8, Intel Corp fell $3/8 to $136-3/8 and International Business Machines Corp dipped $3/8 to $139. General Motors, which fell $1-1/4 in New York on Tuesday, was up $1/4 to $57, while Ford added $1/8 to $32-1/8. Chrysler was unchanged at $29-1/4.

"The techs will open lower, but the fact is that the sector has been getting clobbered for weeks," said Larry Wachtel, analyst at Prudential Securities. "But they may snap back later in the day just to show they're not ready to go to hell in a handbasket because of something in the papers."
He said that even if the CPI were on target this morning, it did not mean that the Fed would not raise rates.
"The key word here is pre-emptive strike," he said. "The Fed is saying 'Sure, inflation is good now. We don't want it to get worse. If economic trends quicken, we will pull the trigger.'"
The dollar edged up in Tokyo and was perched just above 1.68 marks in Europe.
U.S. Treasuries were higher, with the long bond up 8/32 to yield 6.94 percent.
The Wall Street Journal's "Heard on the Street" column said a bear market may have already descended upon technology stocks, which could spell more trouble ahead for the rest of the share market.
The New York Times Market Place writes that investors are starting to question the hefty share prices of the once high-flying high techs.
